criteria.descriptor: Correctly states that the DPO loss depends only on the margin (difference of log-ratios) and explains the shared-token/probability-displacement mechanism accurately; gets the direction of beta right (higher beta = tighter to reference/less drift); describes DPOP or an SFT/NLL anchor correctly. No incorrect claims (e.g. that DPO is buggy, that lower beta reduces drift, or that a falling chosen log-prob alone proves an error).

Covers all three requested parts — mechanism, why the objective permits it, and concrete fixes with trade-offs — and touches the beta role, the data (edit-distance) trigger, at least one likelihood-anchoring fix, and the need for eval/KL guardrails rather than trusting the margin.

Justifies each remediation with a mechanism-linked trade-off (e.g. why higher beta trades margin for stability, why anchoring the chosen likelihood targets the exact failure) rather than listing fixes; connects the margin-only objective to the observed symptoms.

Clear, well-structured explanation using correct terminology (implicit reward, log-ratio, margin, implicit KL, reference model); a grader can follow the causal chain from objective to symptom to fix without ambiguity.

expected_answer_points: The DPO loss is a function only of the difference of the two log-ratios (the margin), so it constrains relative ordering, not absolute likelihood — the loss can fall while the chosen log-prob falls, as long as the rejected falls faster.

Because chosen and rejected pairs share most tokens (small edit distance), the gradient suppressing the rejected sequence also pushes down shared tokens of the chosen sequence, displacing probability mass to unseen/off-distribution continuations and causing degeneration.

beta is the only term anchoring the policy to the reference (an implicit KL constraint); beta = 0.1 is weak, so raising beta reduces drift/degeneration at the cost of a smaller margin and slower learning — and correctly notes higher beta means less deviation.

Add an explicit likelihood anchor on the chosen response — DPO-Positive (DPOP) penalty keeping chosen log-prob at/above reference, or an auxiliary SFT/NLL loss on the chosen (RPO-style) — directly fixing the failure, with the trade-off of an extra hyperparameter that can shrink the margin.
Identify low-edit-distance preference pairs as the specific trigger and propose data curation/filtering or routing such pairs to DPOP.

Recognise the reward margin / training loss is not a sufficient quality signal and add guardrails: track chosen and rejected log-probs separately, KL from reference, and a real generation eval or reward-model score.

Note the falling chosen log-prob is not inherently pathological (only relative reward orders the responses) but becomes harmful once probability mass leaves the data manifold — hence anchoring absolute chosen likelihood is the right response.
common_pitfalls: Claiming DPO is broken or that a decreasing chosen log-prob by itself proves a bug — missing that the objective legitimately constrains only the margin.
Getting the beta direction backwards: suggesting a lower beta to 'strengthen the preference signal', which actually loosens the anchor to the reference and worsens drift.
Attributing the whole problem to overfitting or learning rate without identifying the margin-only objective plus shared-token displacement as the root mechanism.
Recommending a full switch to PPO/online RLHF as the only remedy, overlooking that a cheap explicit anchor (DPOP or an auxiliary SFT loss on the chosen) directly addresses the failure.
Trusting the falling loss and rising reward margin as evidence of success and never proposing generation-quality, reward-model, or KL-from-reference guardrails.
Ignoring the low-edit-distance property of the data, which is the specific documented trigger, and so missing the data-curation and DPOP-routing remedies.
reference_answer:
This is the classic DPO likelihood-displacement / degeneration failure, and the curves are consistent with it rather than a bug.

Mechanism and why the loss permits it: the DPO loss is -log sigma( beta * [ (log pi_theta(y_w|x) - log pi_ref(y_w|x)) - (log pi_theta(y_l|x) - log pi_ref(y_l|x)) ] ). It depends only on the *difference* of the two log-ratios — the margin. Nothing in it pins the absolute likelihood of the chosen response, so the loss keeps falling as long as the rejected log-prob drops faster than the chosen. A rising reward margin with a *falling* chosen log-prob is therefore fully consistent with the objective, not a contradiction. Because your pairs are near-identical edits (small edit distance), chosen and rejected share most tokens; the gradient that suppresses the rejected sequence also pushes down those shared tokens in the chosen sequence, and the displaced probability mass leaks to unseen, off-distribution continuations. That is why generations degenerate (shorter, repetitive) even as the margin looks great.

beta is the only anchor: beta = 0.1 is a weak implicit-KL constraint tying pi_theta to pi_ref, so the policy is free to drift. Raising beta (e.g. 0.3-0.5) tightens the constraint — less degeneration, but smaller preference gains and slower learning.

Fixes with trade-offs:
- Anchor the chosen likelihood: DPO-Positive (DPOP) adds a penalty like max(0, log(pi_ref(y_w) / pi_theta(y_w))) so the chosen log-prob cannot fall below reference; equivalently add a small NLL/SFT loss on y_w (RPO-style). Directly targets the failure; costs a hyperparameter to tune and can shrink the margin if weighted too heavily.
- Curate data: this failure is specifically triggered by low-edit-distance pairs — filter or downweight them, or route them through DPOP.
- Lower the learning rate; DPO degenerates quickly when LR is too high, at the cost of slower convergence.
- Stop trusting margin/loss as the quality signal: log chosen and rejected log-probs separately and KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), and gate promotion on a real generation eval or reward-model score.

Note: a falling chosen log-prob is not intrinsically wrong — only the relative implicit reward matters for the ordering — but here it has gone far enough that mass is escaping the data manifold, so anchoring the absolute likelihood of the chosen response is the correct fix.
